phy_ocra.0.0.summary: Our model of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence appeared: from Dalton's solid spheres, to Thomson's **plum pudding model**, to Rutherford's **nuclear model** (from the alpha particle scattering experiment), to Bohr's electrons in **fixed energy levels (shells)**, and later the discovery of the neutron by Chadwick. Today the atom is described as a tiny, dense, **positively charged nucleus** containing almost all of the mass, surrounded by **negatively charged electrons**, with the nucleus about 100 000 times smaller in radius than the atom. Atoms have a typical radius of about **1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m**, and small molecules are a similar order of magnitude, around 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁹ m.

core.p: A scientific model is a simplified way of describing something we cannot see directly. A model is kept while it explains the evidence. When a new experiment produces results the model cannot explain, scientists modify or replace it. The history of the atom is the classic example of this process.
bullets: Models are **tested by experiments** that make predictions.
If results **disagree** with predictions, the model must change.
New models must explain **both the old and the new evidence**.
New ideas are checked by other scientists (**peer review**) and by repeating experiments before they are accepted.
Better technology (e.g. radioactive sources, detectors) often makes new evidence possible.

callouts.p: Questions on this point ask both HOW the model changed (what was new) and WHY (what evidence forced the change). Always give both.

core.p: In the early 1800s John Dalton proposed that all matter is made of tiny particles called atoms, which he pictured as solid spheres that cannot be divided. Different elements were made of different kinds of atom.
bullets: Atoms pictured as **tiny solid spheres** that cannot be broken up.
Each element has its own type of atom.
Explained why elements combine in fixed ratios in compounds.
Replaced when the electron was discovered, showing atoms contain smaller particles.

core.p: In 1897 J.J. Thomson discovered the electron, a tiny negatively charged particle much lighter than an atom. Because atoms are neutral overall, there had to be positive charge too. He suggested the plum pudding model.
bullets: Evidence: discovery of the **electron**, showing atoms are **not indivisible**.
Model: a **ball of positive charge** with **negative electrons embedded** in it, like plums in a pudding.
Mass and positive charge spread **evenly** throughout the atom.
Overall the atom is **neutral** because the charges balance.
There is **no nucleus** in this model.

fig.cap: Thomson's plum pudding model: negative electrons embedded in a sphere of spread-out positive charge. There is no nucleus.

core.p: In 1909 Geiger and Marsden, working with Ernest Rutherford, fired a beam of alpha particles (small, fast, positively charged particles) at a very thin sheet of gold foil and recorded where they went using a detector. If the plum pudding model were right, the spread-out charge would be too weak to deflect the heavy alpha particles much, so they should all pass almost straight through.
bullets: **Most alpha particles passed straight through** the foil.
**Some were deflected** through small angles.
A **very small number (about 1 in 8000) bounced back** through more than 90 degrees.
The back-scattering could not be explained by the plum pudding model.
Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back.

head: Observation
Conclusion
rows: Most alpha particles went straight through
Most of the atom is empty space
The centre of the atom is positively charged (it repels the positive alpha particles)
A very few bounced straight back
The positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus

callouts.p: 6-mark answers expect each observation linked to its own conclusion. Keep the three pairs separate and complete.

core.p: To explain the scattering results, Rutherford (1911) proposed the nuclear model, which replaced the plum pudding model.
bullets: A **tiny, positively charged nucleus** at the centre.
**Almost all the mass** of the atom is in the nucleus.
**Electrons** orbit the nucleus at a relatively large distance.
Most of the atom is **empty space**.
Problem: it could not explain why orbiting electrons did not spiral into the nucleus, or why atoms emit only particular colours of light.

core.p: Niels Bohr (1913) improved the nuclear model. He suggested electrons can only orbit the nucleus at certain fixed distances, called energy levels or shells. His calculations agreed with experimental observations of the light given out by atoms.
bullets: Electrons occupy **fixed energy levels (shells)** at specific distances from the nucleus.
Electrons can **move between levels** by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation.
Explained why atoms are **stable** and why they emit light only at **specific wavelengths (line spectra)**.
Theoretical calculations agreed with experimental results, so the model was accepted.

core.p: Later experiments showed that the positive charge of the nucleus is carried by particles called protons. In 1932 James Chadwick provided evidence for the neutron, a neutral particle in the nucleus. This explained why the mass of most nuclei was greater than the mass of their protons alone.
bullets: **Proton**: relative charge +1, relative mass 1, in the nucleus.
**Neutron**: relative charge 0, relative mass 1, in the nucleus (Chadwick, 1932).
**Electron**: relative charge -1, very small mass (about 1/2000), in shells around the nucleus.
An atom has **equal numbers of protons and electrons**, so it has **no overall charge**.

core.p: Learn the sequence and the key evidence for each step, because exam questions often ask you to put models in order or to say what evidence led to a change.
bullets: Each new model kept what still worked and changed what the new evidence contradicted.
The most important single change for this spec point: **plum pudding to nuclear model**, caused by **alpha scattering**.

rows: Fixed ratios of elements in compounds

core.p: The atom is now described as a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom, but contains almost all of its mass.
bullets: **Nucleus**: positively charged, contains protons and neutrons, contains **almost all the mass**.
**Electrons**: negatively charged, arranged in shells around the nucleus.
Radius of nucleus is about **1/100 000 (10⁻⁵)** of the radius of the atom.
Atom radius about **1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m**; nuclear radius about **1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m**.
So the atom is **mostly empty space**.

callouts.p: An atom consists of a small, positively charged nucleus, containing almost all of the mass, surrounded by negatively charged electrons; the radius of the nucleus is much smaller than that of the atom.

core.h: Sizes of atoms and small molecules
core.p: You need to recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules as an order of magnitude. These sizes are so small that standard form is essential.
bullets: Typical **atomic radius ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m** (0.1 nanometres).
Small molecules (e.g. H₂O, CO₂) are of the **same order of magnitude**, roughly 10⁻¹⁰ m to 10⁻⁹ m across.
Nucleus radius ≈ **1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m**, about 100 000 times smaller than the atom.
About 10 million atoms side by side would span 1 mm.

callouts.p: Atom radius about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; small molecules similar order; nucleus about 1/100 000 of the atom.

core.p: Questions often ask you to compare sizes or work out how many times bigger one thing is than another. Divide the larger by the smaller and use powers of ten.
bullets: Atom / nucleus = 10⁻¹⁰ / 10⁻¹⁵ = **10⁵ = 100 000**.
Dividing powers of ten: **subtract the indices**.
If the nucleus were a 1 cm marble, the atom would be about 1 km across.
An order of magnitude is a factor of 10.

callouts.p: 10⁻¹⁵ is SMALLER than 10⁻¹⁰. The more negative the power, the smaller the number.

analogy.p: If an atom were blown up to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a marble on the centre spot, and the electrons would be like tiny specks of dust buzzing around the outer stands. Almost all the stadium's 'mass' would be in that marble, and the rest would be empty space. This explains why alpha particles mostly pass straight through. It breaks down because electrons do not fly around in neat paths like dust, they occupy fixed energy levels, and the 'empty space' is not empty in an everyday sense: it is filled with the electric fields that push alpha particles away from the nucleus.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element; a positive nucleus surrounded by negative electrons, with no overall charge.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons and almost all the mass.
A negatively charged particle (relative charge -1) of very small mass, found in shells around the nucleus.
A particle in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
A particle in the nucleus with no charge and relative mass 1.
Thomson's model: a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
Rutherford's model: a tiny positive nucleus with electrons around it; mostly empty space.
A positively charged particle made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, used in Rutherford's scattering experiment.
Firing alpha particles at thin gold foil and observing how they were deflected; evidence for the nucleus.
A fixed distance from the nucleus at which electrons can orbit (Bohr).
A simplified representation used to explain observations and make predictions.
The size of a quantity as a power of ten.
A way of writing numbers as A × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ A < 10.
Two or more atoms bonded together; small molecules are about 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁹ m in size.
Checking of scientific work by other experts before it is published and accepted.

mistakes.w: The plum pudding model has a nucleus.
mistakes.r: The plum pudding model has no nucleus; positive charge is spread throughout.
Most went straight through; only a very small number bounced back.

mistakes.w: Alpha particles went straight through because they are small.
mistakes.r: Most of the atom is empty space.

mistakes.w: Alpha particles were deflected by electrons.
mistakes.r: They were repelled by the positively charged nucleus.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is half the size of the atom.
mistakes.r: The nucleus radius is about 1/100 000 of the atom's radius.
Atoms are about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; 10⁻¹⁵ m is the nucleus.

mistakes.w: The mass of the atom is spread evenly.
mistakes.r: Almost all of the mass is concentrated in the nucleus.
Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) discovered the nucleus; Bohr proposed energy levels.

mistakes.w: Scientists changed the model because they had a new idea.
mistakes.r: The model changed because new experimental evidence could not be explained by the old model.

exam.q: State the typical radius of an atom.
exam.tip: Give a unit; 0.1 nm also accepted.

exam.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
model: a sphere (ball) of positive charge
with (negative) electrons embedded in it
exam.tip: Mention both the positive part and the electrons.

exam.q: State where almost all of the mass of an atom is found.
model: in the nucleus
exam.tip: One word answer is fine.

exam.q: Name the scientist who discovered the electron.
model: (J.J.) Thomson
exam.tip: Do not confuse with Rutherford.

exam.q: In the alpha scattering experiment most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this tell you about the atom?
model: most of the atom is empty space
exam.tip: Match observation to conclusion.

exam.q: Explain why a few alpha particles were deflected back towards the source.
model: they came close to (or hit head-on) a small, massive nucleus
which is positively charged so it repelled the positive alpha particles
exam.tip: Mention both positive charge and concentrated mass.

exam.q: The radius of an atom is 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and the radius of its nucleus is 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Calculate how many times larger the atom is than the nucleus.
exam.tip: Subtract indices when dividing powers of ten.

exam.q: Describe the contribution of Niels Bohr to the model of the atom.
model: electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances / in energy levels or shells
his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations (spectra)
exam.tip: Two separate points: what he proposed and why it was accepted.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom in the nuclear model, including the relative size of the nucleus.
model: positively charged nucleus at the centre containing almost all the mass
negatively charged electrons around the nucleus (in shells)
nucleus radius is about 1/100 000 of the atom radius / atom mostly empty space
exam.tip: Use the words 'positively charged' and 'almost all the mass'.

exam.q: Describe how and why the model of the atom changed from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model. Refer to the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment in your answer.
model: plum pudding: sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded, mass spread out
alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil
most went straight through, so most of the atom is empty space
some were deflected, so the centre must be positively charged
a very few bounced back, so the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
the plum pudding model predicted all would pass almost straight through, so it could not explain the results and was replaced by the nuclear model
exam.tip: Structure: old model, experiment, three observation-conclusion pairs, why the old model failed.

worked.q: A nucleus has a radius of 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The atom's radius is 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. If a model is built with the nucleus as a ball of radius 1 cm, what would be the radius of the model atom?
A water molecule is about 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m across. How many molecules lined up would stretch 3 mm?
Model answer: explain why the plum pudding model could not explain alpha particles bouncing back from gold foil.
steps: In the plum pudding model the positive charge and mass are spread thinly throughout the atom
So the electric force on a passing alpha particle would be weak and spread out
The heavy, fast alpha particles would therefore only be deflected by tiny angles
Bouncing back needs a large repulsive force from a concentrated positive charge with a large mass
worked.ans: Only a small, dense, positively charged nucleus can produce enough repulsion to turn an alpha particle back, so the plum pudding model was replaced.

phy_ocra.0.1.summary: **Density** tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of volume of a material, and is calculated with density = mass / volume. The particle model explains why solids and liquids are usually much denser than gases: in solids and liquids the particles are touching, while in a gas they are far apart with mostly empty space between them. In PAG P1 you find the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids by measuring mass with a balance and volume with a ruler, a measuring cylinder or a displacement (eureka) can.

core.p: Density is a property of a material, not of a particular object. A small iron nail and a large iron girder have the same density, because each cubic centimetre of iron has the same mass. Density compares materials fairly by asking how much mass is squeezed into the same volume.
bullets: **Density** = mass per unit volume
A **dense** material has a lot of mass in a small volume (e.g. lead, gold)
A material with **low density** has little mass in a large volume (e.g. air, polystyrene)
Cutting an object in half halves the mass AND the volume, so the **density stays the same**
Density depends on **how heavy the particles are** and **how closely they are packed**

callouts.p: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance: density = mass / volume.
A big log is heavier than a small pebble but the log is less dense. Density is about mass in each unit of volume, not total mass.

core.p: OCR gives the equation as density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) / volume (m³). The symbol for density is the Greek letter rho, written ρ. You must recall this equation; it is not always given on the equation sheet.
bullets: Mass m in **kilograms (kg)** or grams (g)
Volume V in **cubic metres (m³)** or cubic centimetres (cm³)
Density in **kg/m³** or **g/cm³**
Use matching units: kg with m³ gives kg/m³; g with cm³ gives g/cm³
Water has a density of about **1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³**

core.p: Unit conversions are where most marks are lost. A cubic metre is a cube 100 cm on each side, so it holds 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³, not 100 cm³.
bullets: 1 cm³ = **1 ml**; 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 0.001 m³
To convert g/cm³ to kg/m³, **multiply by 1000**
To convert kg/m³ to g/cm³, **divide by 1000**
Example: aluminium 2.7 g/cm³ = **2700 kg/m³**

callouts.p: Do not divide cm³ by 100 to get m³. You must divide by 100 three times, i.e. by 1 000 000.

core.p: In a solid, the particles (atoms or molecules) are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. They are touching their neighbours and are usually arranged in a regular pattern. They cannot move from place to place; they only vibrate about fixed positions.
bullets: Particles **close together and touching**
**Regular arrangement** (a lattice) in most solids
Particles **vibrate about fixed positions**
**Strong forces** between particles
Fixed shape and fixed volume; cannot be compressed
Very little empty space, so **high density**

core.p: In a liquid, particles are still touching, so there is still very little space between them, but they are in a random arrangement and can slide past each other. That is why liquids flow and take the shape of their container but keep the same volume.
bullets: Particles **close together and touching**
**Random (irregular) arrangement**
Particles **move around and slide past each other**
Forces weaker than in a solid but still significant
Fixed volume, no fixed shape; almost incompressible
Density usually **similar to, slightly less than, the solid**

core.p: In a gas, the particles are far apart with lots of empty space between them. They move quickly in random directions and the forces between them are very weak. Because the same mass of particles is spread through a far larger volume, gases have very low densities.
bullets: Particles **far apart**, mostly empty space
**Random arrangement**
Particles **move fast in random directions**
Forces between particles are **very weak**
No fixed shape or volume; easily **compressed**
**Very low density**, about 1000 times less than the liquid (air is about 1.2 kg/m³)

core.p: The particles themselves do not change size or mass when a substance changes state. What changes is how far apart they are. Density = mass / volume, so the same mass taking up more volume means lower density. This is the explanation the mark scheme wants: link spacing of particles to volume, and volume to density.
bullets: Same particles, same mass in every state
Solid and liquid: particles touching, so **small volume, high density**
Gas: particles far apart, so **large volume, low density**
Solid usually slightly denser than liquid because particles are **packed more closely in a regular pattern**
Exception: **ice is less dense than water**, which is why ice floats
Mass is **conserved** when a substance changes state; only the volume changes

callouts.p: State the arrangement in each state, then the spacing, then link spacing to volume for the same mass, then conclude about density using ρ = m / V.

core.p: Exam questions often give density and ask for mass or volume. Rearrange before substituting, and always write the equation, the substitution, the answer and the unit.
bullets: Convert to consistent units **before** substituting
Give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures (usually the same as the data)
Include the **unit** every time

callouts.p: Even if your final answer is wrong, writing the equation and a correct substitution usually earns marks.

core.h: PAG P1: density of a regular solid
core.p: For a regular shape such as a cuboid, you can calculate the volume from measured dimensions. The mass is found with a top-pan balance.
bullets: Measure the **mass** with a **top-pan balance** (zeroed first)
Measure **length, width and height** with a ruler (or vernier calipers / micrometer for small objects)
Calculate **volume = length × width × height** for a cuboid
Calculate **density = mass / volume**
Repeat measurements and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of random errors
Use the most precise instrument available (calipers have resolution 0.1 mm or better)

core.h: PAG P1: density of an irregular solid
core.p: An irregular object such as a stone has no simple formula for volume, so you measure the volume of water it displaces. A displacement (eureka) can is filled until water just stops dripping from the spout; when the object is lowered in, the water pushed out is collected in a measuring cylinder. The volume of water displaced equals the volume of the object.
bullets: Measure the **mass** of the dry object on a balance first
Fill the **eureka can** until water drips from the spout, then wait until it stops
Place an empty **measuring cylinder** under the spout
**Lower the object gently on a thread** so no water splashes out
Read the volume of **displaced water** in the cylinder at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Alternative: put water in a measuring cylinder, record the volume, add the object and record the new volume; **volume of object = final − initial**
Calculate **density = mass / volume**

callouts.p: Volume of water displaced = volume of the object (as long as the object is fully submerged).

fig.cap: Eureka (displacement) can method. The can is filled to the spout first; the water pushed out when the object is lowered in on a thread is collected, and its volume equals the object's volume.

core.h: PAG P1: density of a liquid
core.p: For a liquid, mass and volume are both measured using a measuring cylinder and a balance. The key idea is to find the mass of the liquid only, not the mass of the container.
bullets: Place an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and **zero (tare) the balance**
Pour in liquid and read the **volume** at eye level from the **bottom of the meniscus**
Read the **mass** of liquid from the balance
Or: mass of liquid = (mass of cylinder + liquid) − (mass of empty cylinder)
Calculate **density = mass / volume**
Repeat with different volumes; a graph of mass against volume gives a straight line through the origin whose **gradient = density**

fig.cap: Finding the density of a liquid: tare the balance with the empty measuring cylinder, add liquid, read the volume at eye level and the mass from the balance.

core.h: Accuracy, precision and errors in PAG P1
core.p: Density practicals combine two measurements, so errors in either mass or volume affect the result. Good technique reduces these errors.
bullets: **Zero the balance** before use to avoid a zero error
Read measuring cylinders at **eye level** to avoid **parallax error**
Use the **smallest measuring cylinder** that holds the volume, for better resolution
Make sure the object is **fully submerged** and that no air bubbles cling to it
In the eureka can, **do not drop** the object, as splashing loses water
Dry the object or weigh it before putting it in water
**Repeat and average** to reduce random errors; identify and discard anomalous results

callouts.p: If the can is not filled right up to the spout before adding the object, some displaced water only raises the level and is never collected, so the measured volume is too small and the density too large.

core.h: Using density to identify materials and predict floating
core.p: Because every pure substance has its own density, measuring density can help identify a material, for example checking whether a ring is pure gold. An object floats in a fluid if its overall density is less than the density of the fluid.
bullets: Compare calculated density with a **table of known densities**
Gold ≈ 19 300 kg/m³, aluminium ≈ 2700 kg/m³, water ≈ 1000 kg/m³
Objects **less dense than water float**; objects more dense sink
**Ice (about 920 kg/m³) floats** on water because it is less dense
Hot air rises because heated air expands, so the same mass occupies more volume, so its density decreases

analogy.p: Imagine the same 30 students in a room. Standing shoulder to shoulder in neat rows is a solid: lots of people per square metre. Standing shoulder to shoulder but milling around is a liquid: still crowded, still about the same number per square metre. Spreading out across a huge sports hall and running about is a gas: the same 30 people, but very few per square metre. Density is the number of people (mass) per square metre (volume). Where it breaks down: real particles in a gas are much further apart relative to their size than people in a hall, the gaps are truly empty space, and density also depends on the mass of each particle, not just how many there are.

terms.d: Mass per unit volume of a substance; density = mass / volume.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
The amount of space an object takes up, measured in m³ or cm³.
SI unit of density: kilograms of mass in each cubic metre.
Laboratory unit of density; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Model in which all matter is made of tiny particles whose arrangement and motion explain properties of solids, liquids and gases.
State with particles touching in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
State with particles touching in a random arrangement, able to slide past each other.
State with particles far apart in a random arrangement, moving quickly in random directions.
An object with a regular shape whose volume can be calculated from its measured dimensions.
An object with no regular shape, whose volume is found by displacement of water.
A displacement can with a spout used to collect the water displaced by an object.
Method of finding volume: the volume of liquid pushed aside equals the volume of the submerged object.
The curved surface of a liquid in a tube; read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Electronic instrument used to measure mass; zero it before use.
Error caused by reading a scale from an angle instead of at eye level.
To reset a balance to zero with a container on it so only the contents are measured.

mistakes.w: Density is how heavy something is.
mistakes.r: Density is mass per unit volume.

mistakes.w: Gas particles are smaller, so gases are less dense.
mistakes.r: The particles are the same size; in a gas they are far apart, so the same mass takes up a much larger volume.

mistakes.w: Multiplying mass by volume to find density.
Liquids are much less dense than solids because particles are far apart.
mistakes.r: Particles in a liquid are still touching, so densities of a substance as solid and liquid are similar.

mistakes.w: Measuring the volume of an irregular object with a ruler.
mistakes.r: Use displacement of water in a eureka can or measuring cylinder.

mistakes.w: Reading the measuring cylinder from above.
mistakes.r: Read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error.

mistakes.w: The mass of a substance changes when it melts or boils.
mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; only the spacing of particles, and so the volume and density, changes.

mistakes.w: Answer with no unit, or g/cm³ when mass was in kg and volume in m³.
mistakes.r: Units must match the quantities used, e.g. kg/m³.

exam.q: State the equation that links density, mass and volume.
model: density = mass / volume
exam.tip: Words or symbols are both accepted; ρ = m / V.

exam.q: A block has a mass of 0.54 kg and a volume of 0.0002 m³. Calculate its density.
model: = 2700 kg/m³
exam.tip: Write the substitution before the answer to secure the first mark.

exam.q: Convert a density of 7.9 g/cm³ into kg/m³.
model: 7900 kg/m³
exam.tip: Multiply by 1000 when going from g/cm³ to kg/m³.

exam.q: A piece of cork has a density of 240 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.005 m³. Calculate its mass.
model: m = ρ × V
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then substitute.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why the density of steam is much lower than the density of water.
model: Particles in steam (gas) are far apart; particles in water (liquid) are touching
So the same mass of steam occupies a much larger volume
Density = mass / volume, so the density of steam is lower
exam.tip: Always link spacing to volume and then volume to density.

exam.q: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a solid.
model: Particles touching in a regular arrangement
Particles vibrate about fixed positions
exam.tip: Arrangement and movement are separate marks; give both.

exam.q: Suggest why the density of a substance as a solid is usually only slightly greater than as a liquid.
model: In both states particles are touching / close together
So the volume of a given mass changes only slightly (solid particles slightly more closely packed)
exam.tip: Avoid saying liquid particles are far apart.

exam.q: Describe how a student could find the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
model: Measure the mass of the stone using a top-pan balance (zeroed)
Fill a eureka can with water up to the spout and let it stop dripping
Place a measuring cylinder under the spout
Lower the stone gently into the water on a thread so it is fully submerged
Measure the volume of displaced water at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus; this equals the volume of the stone
Calculate density = mass / volume, repeat and find a mean
exam.tip: Six-mark method answers need a logical order: mass, volume, calculation, improving reliability.

exam.q: Describe how to find the density of a liquid such as cooking oil.
model: Place an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and tare it (or record its mass)
Pour in oil and read the volume at eye level
Read the mass of the oil (or subtract mass of empty cylinder)
Calculate density = mass / volume
exam.tip: Make clear you find the mass of the liquid only.

exam.q: A student did not fill the eureka can up to the spout before lowering in the object. Explain the effect on the calculated density.
model: Less water is collected than the object's volume, so the measured volume is too small
So the calculated density is too large
exam.tip: Say the direction of the error, not just that it is inaccurate.

exam.q: A cube of side 2.0 cm has a mass of 21.6 g. Calculate its density in kg/m³.
model: Density = 21.6 / 8.0 = 2.7 g/cm³
= 2700 kg/m³
exam.tip: Work in g and cm³ first, then convert the final density.

worked.q: A rectangular block of metal measures 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm and has a mass of 316 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³ and kg/m³ and use the table value 7900 kg/m³ to suggest the metal.
steps: This matches the density of iron/steel
worked.ans: 7.9 g/cm³ = 7900 kg/m³, so the block is probably iron (steel).

worked.q: A stone of mass 150 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 40 cm³ to 100 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone.
A tank holds 0.30 m³ of oil of density 920 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of the oil.
